documentNotes.title: Please read this carefully:
documentNotes.statement:
1. Every student receives problem sheets in English and/or in his/her native language, answer sheets, millimeter block papers, and scratch sheets.
2. The time available is five hours for the data analysis and observation competitions. There are three data analysis problems, and two observation problems.
3. Use only the materials provided.
4. Fill in the boxes at the top of each sheet of paper with your country code and your student code.
5. Use only the front side of **answer sheets**. Write only inside the boxed area.
6. Begin answering each question on a separate sheet.
7. Numerical results should be written with as many digits as are appropriate.
8. Write on **the answer sheets and the millimeter block papers** whatever you consider is required for the solution of each question. Please express your answer primarily in term of equations, numbers, figures, and plots. If necessary provide your answers with concise text. Full credit will be given to correct answer with detailed steps for each question. Underline your final result.
9. At the end of the exam place the answer sheets and the millimeter block papers inside the envelope and leave everything on your desk.

problems.title: Virgo Cluster
problems.statement:
The Virgo cluster of galaxies is the nearest large cluster which extends over nearly 10 degrees across the sky and contains a number of bright galaxies. It is very interesting to find the distance to Virgo and to deduce certain cosmological information from it. The table below provides the distance estimates using various distance indicators (listed in the left column). The right column lists the mean distance $d_i$ ± the standard deviation $s_i$.

| $i$ | Distance Indicator | Virgo Distance (Mpc |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cepheids | $14.9 \pm 1.2$ |
| 2 | Novae | $21.1 \pm 3.9$ |
| 3 | Planetary Nebulae | $15.2 \pm 1.1$ |
| 4 | Globular Cluster | $18.8 \pm 3.8$ |
| 5 | Surface Brightness Fluctuation | $15.9 \pm 0.9$ |
| 6 | Tully-Fisher relation | $15.8 \pm 1.5$ |
| 7 | Faber-Jackson relation | $16.8 \pm 2.4$ |
| 8 | Type Ia Supernovae | $19.4 \pm 5.0$ |

parts.statement:
By applying a weighted mean, compute the average distance (which can be taken as an estimate to the distance to Virgo)

$$d_{avg} = \frac{\sum_i \frac{d_i}{s_i^2}}{\sum_i \frac{1}{s_i^2}}$$

where the sum runs over the eight distance indicator used.
What is the uncertainty (rms) (in unit of Mpc) in that estimate?
Spectra of the galaxies in Virgo indicate an average recession velocity of 1136 km/sec for the cluster. Can you estimate the Hubble constant $H_0$ and its uncertainty (rms)?

answer.note: Official result: H0 = 72 ± 2 km/sec/Mpc (71.9 km/sec/Mpc before rounding, uncertainty 2.4 km/sec/Mpc).

parts.statement: What is the Hubble Time (age of the universe) using the value of Hubble constant you found and the uncertainty (rms)?

answer.note: Official result: 13.6 Gyr with an uncertainty of 3.35%, i.e. 0.45 Gyr.

solution.statement:
1. From table above, we have $\sum_i \frac{d_i}{s_i^2} = 56.1082$ and $\sum_i \frac{1}{s_i^2} = 3.5485$, so:

$$d_{avg} = \frac{56.1082}{3.5485}\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 15.81\ \mathrm{Mpc}$$

**(30%)**

2. The uncertainty (rms):

$$s_d = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\sum_i \frac{1}{s_i^2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{3.5485}}\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 0.53\ \mathrm{Mpc}$$

$$d_{Virgo} = 15.81 \pm 0.53\ \mathrm{Mpc}$$

**(10%)**

3. Hubble constant

$$H_0 = \frac{v}{d_{avg}} = \frac{1136\ \mathrm{km/s}}{15.81\ \mathrm{Mpc}} = 71.9\ \mathrm{km/sec/Mpc}$$

**(15%)**

Uncertainty:

$$s_{H_0} = \frac{s_d}{d_{avg}} H_0 = \frac{0.53}{15.81} \times 71.85 = 0.0335 \times 71.85 = 2.4\ \mathrm{km/sec/Mpc}$$

**(15%)**

**Hubble constant:** $H_0 = 72 \pm 2\ km/\mathrm{sec}/Mpc$ **(5%)**

4. Hubble time:

$$H_0^{-1} = \frac{1}{H_0} = \frac{1}{71.85\ \mathrm{km/sec/Mpc}} \times 3.086 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{km/Mpc} = 4.29 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{sec} = 13.6\ \mathrm{Gyr}$$

**(20%)**

Uncertainty is 3.35% which is 0.45 Gyr. **(5%)**

problems.title: Determination of stellar masses in a visual binary system
problems.statement:
The star α-Centauri (Rigel Kentaurus) is a triple star which consists of two main-sequence stars α-Centauri A and α-Centauri B representing visual binary system, and the third star, called Proxima Centauri, which is smaller and fainter than the other two stars. The angular distance between α-Centauri A and α-Centauri B is 17.59”. The binary system has an orbital period of 79.24 years. The visual magnitudes of α-Centauri A and α-Centauri B are -0.01 and 1.34 respectively. Their color indices are 0.65 and 0.85 respectively. Use the data below to answer the following questions.

Data for main-sequence stars

| $(B-V)_0$ | $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ | $BC$ |
|---|---|---|
| -0.25 | 24500 | 2.30 |
| -0.23 | 21000 | 2.15 |
| -0.20 | 17700 | 1.80 |
| -0.15 | 14000 | 1.20 |
| -0.10 | 11800 | 0.61 |
| -0.05 | 10500 | 0.33 |
| 0.00 | 9480 | 0.15 |
| 0.10 | 8530 | 0.04 |
| 0.20 | 7910 | 0 |
| 0.30 | 7450 | 0 |
| 0.40 | 6800 | 0 |
| 0.50 | 6310 | 0.03 |
| 0.60 | 5910 | 0.07 |
| 0.70 | 5540 | 0.12 |
| 0.80 | 5330 | 0.19 |
| 0.90 | 5090 | 0.28 |
| 1.00 | 4840 | 0.40 |
| 1.20 | 4350 | 0.75 |

$BC$=Bolometric Correction, $(B-V)_0$=Intrinsic Color

Questions:

answer.note: A plot; see the official solution.

parts.statement: Determine the apparent bolometric magnitudes of α-Centauri A and α-Centauri B using the corresponding curve.

answer.value: m_bol(α Cen A) = -0.11, m_bol(α Cen B) = 1.09 (BC = 0.10 and 0.25 read from the curve)

parts.statement: Calculate the mass of each star.

problems.statementAfterParts:
*Notes*:

1. **Bolometric correction** (BC) is a correction that must be made to the apparent magnitude of an object in order to convert an object's visible magnitude to its bolometric magnitude:

$$BC = m_v - m_{bol} \quad \text{or} \quad BC = M_v - M_{bol}$$

2. **Luminosity mass relation** : $M_{bol} = -10.2\log\left(\frac{\mathrm{M}}{\mathrm{M}_{\odot}}\right) + 4.9$

solution.statement:
1

**(20%)**

2.

⊙ For α Cen. A. , its colour index is given by $B - V = 0.65$. Then, by taking the line that intersecting the above curve we find $BC = 0.10$. **(10%)**

⊙ For α Cen. B. , its colour index is given by $B - V = 0.85$. Then, by taking the line that intersecting the above curve we find $BC = 0.25$. **(10%)**

From the relation $m_{\mathrm{v}} - m_{\mathrm{bol}} = BC$ it is then obtained,

⊙ For α Cen. A, $m_{\mathrm{v}} = -0.01$, we get $m_{\mathrm{bol}} = -0.01 - 0.10 = -0.11$ **(10%)**

⊙ For α Cen. B, $m_{\mathrm{v}} = 1.34$, we get $m_{\mathrm{bol}} = 1.34 - 0.25 = 1.09$ **(10%)**

3. Periodic orbit of α Centauri star is $P = 79.24$ years and its angle of semi major axis is $\alpha = 17.59''$. From the result 2a we find that the apparent bolometric magnitude of α Centauri A is $m_{\mathrm{bolA}} = -0.11$, while the apparent bolometric magnitude of α Centauri B is $m_{\mathrm{bolB}} = 1.09$. (two decimal places)

*1st iteration :*

Step 1 : Let $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}}$ be the mass of Centauri A and Centauri B stars, respectively. Then, we firstly take $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}} + \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}} = 2$

Step 2 : Inserting the values of $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}} + \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}}$, $P$, and $\alpha$ to the third Kepler equation namely,

$$\left(\frac{\alpha}{p}\right)^3 = \left(\mathcal{M}_A + \mathcal{M}_B\right)P^2$$

One gets $p$, that is

$$p = \left[\frac{\alpha^3}{\left(\mathcal{M}_A + \mathcal{M}_B\right)P^2}\right]^{1/3} = \left[\frac{(17.59)^3}{2(79.24)^2}\right]^{1/3} = \left[0.4334\right]^{1/3} = 0.7568''$$

Step 3 : We determine the magnitude of absolute bolometric using Pogson equation,

$$m_{bol} - M_{bol} = -5 - 5\log p \Longrightarrow M_{bol} = m_{bol} + 5 + 5\log p$$

For α Centauri A:

$$M_{bolA} = m_{bolA} + 5 + 5\log p = -0.11 + 5 + 5\log(0.7568) = -0.11 + 5 - 0.6051 = 4.2849$$

For α Centauri B :

$$M_{bolB} = m_{bolB} + 5 + 5\log p = 1.09 + 5 + 5\log(0.7568) = 1.09 + 5 - 0.6051 = 5.4849$$

Step 4 : We determine the mass of both stars using luminosity mass relation,

$$M_{bol} = -10.2\log\left(\frac{\mathcal{M}}{\mathcal{M}_{\odot}}\right) + 4.9 \Longrightarrow \mathcal{M} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - M_{bol}}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$$

For α Centauri A:

$$\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - M_{bolA}}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - 4.2849}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 1.1490\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$$

For α Centauri B:

$$\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - M_{bolB}}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - 5.4949}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 0.8763\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$$

**(30%)**

*2nd iteration* Repeating the step 1 until 4 and using the previous resulting mass in the first iteration:

Step 1 : $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}} + \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}} = 1.1490 + 0.8763 = 2.0253$

Step 2 : $$p = \left[\frac{\alpha^3}{\left(\mathcal{M}_A + \mathcal{M}_B\right)P^2}\right]^{1/3} = \left[\frac{(17.59)^3}{(2.0253)(79.24)^2}\right]^{1/3} = 0.7536$$

Step 3 : For α Centauri A:

$$M_{bolA} = m_{bolA} + 5 + 5\log p = -0.11 + 5 + 5\log(0.7536) = 4.2757$$

For α Centauri B :

$$M_{bolB} = m_{bolB} + 5 + 5\log p = 1.09 + 5 + 5\log(0.7536) = 5.4757$$

Step 4 : For α Centauri A:

$$\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - M_{bolA}}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - 4.2757}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 1.1513\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$$

For α Centauri B:

$$\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - M_{bolB}}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - 5.4757}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 0.8781\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$$

**(10%)**

*3 rd Iteration* Repeating the step 1 until 4 and using the previous resulting mass in the second iteration:

Step 1 : $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}} + \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}} = 1.1513 + 0.8781 = 2.0294$

Step 2 : $$p = \left[\frac{\alpha^3}{\left(\mathcal{M}_A + \mathcal{M}_B\right)P^2}\right]^{1/3} = \left[\frac{(17.59)^3}{(2.0294)(79.24)^2}\right]^{1/3} = 0.75314$$

Step 3 : For α Centauri A:

$$M_{bolA} = m_{bolA} + 5 + 5\log p = -0.11 + 5 + 5\log(0.7531) = 4.2751$$

For α Centauri B :

$$M_{bolB} = m_{bolB} + 5 + 5\log p = 1.09 + 5 + 5\log(0.7531) = 5.4751$$

Step 4 : For α Centauri A:

$$\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - M_{bolA}}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - 4.2751}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 1.1515\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$$

For α Centauri B:

$$\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - M_{bolB}}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - 5.4751}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 0.8782\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$$

**(0%)**

*4 th Iteration* Repeating the step 1 until 4 and using the previous resulting mass in the third iteration:

Step 1 : $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}} + \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}} = 1.1515 + 0.8782 = 2.0297$

Step 2 : $$p = \left[\frac{\alpha^3}{\left(\mathcal{M}_A + \mathcal{M}_B\right)P^2}\right]^{1/3} = \left[\frac{(17.59)^3}{(2.0297)(79.24)^2}\right]^{1/3} = 0.7531$$

Step 3 : For α Centauri A:

$$M_{bolA} = m_{bolA} + 5 + 5\log p = -0.11 + 5 + 5\log(0.7531) = 4.2753$$

For α Centauri B :

$$M_{bolB} = m_{bolB} + 5 + 5\log p = 1.09 + 5 + 5\log(0.7531) = 5.4743$$

Step 4 : For α Centauri A:

$$\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - M_{bolA}}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - 4.2753}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 1.1517\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$$

For α Centauri B:

$$\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - M_{bolB}}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - 5.4743}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 0.8784\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$$

**(0%)**

*5 th Iteration* Repeating the step 1 until 4 and using the previous resulting mass in the fourth iteration:

Step 1 : $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}} + \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}} = 1.1517 + 0.8784 = 2.0301$

Step 2 : $$p = \left[\frac{\alpha^3}{\left(\mathcal{M}_A + \mathcal{M}_B\right)P^2}\right]^{1/3} = \left[\frac{(17.59)^3}{(2.0301)(79.24)^2}\right]^{1/3} = 0.7530''$$

Step 3 : For α Centauri A:

$$M_{bolA} = m_{bolA} + 5 + 5\log p = -0.11 + 5 + 5\log(0.7530) = 4.2740$$

For α Centauri B :

$$M_{bolB} = m_{bolB} + 5 + 5\log p = 1.10 + 5 + 5\log(0.7530) = 5.4740$$

Step 4 : For α Centauri A:

$$\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - M_{bolA}}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - 4.2740}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 1.1518\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$$

For α Centauri B:

$$\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - M_{bolB}}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 10^{\left(\frac{4.9 - 5.4740}{10.2}\right)}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} = 0.8785\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$$

**(0%)**

The results of the fifth iteration equal the results of the fourth iteration, so

The mass of α Centauri A : $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{A}} = 1.1518\ \mathcal{M}_{\odot}$

The mass of α Centauri B : $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{B}} = 0.8785\ \mathcal{M}_{\odot}$

problems.title: The Age of Meteorite
problems.statement:
The basic equation of radioactive decay can be expressed as:

$$N(t) = N_0 \exp(-\lambda t)$$

where $N(t)$ and $N_0$ are the number of remaining atoms of the radioactive isotope (or parent isotope) at time $t$ and its initial number at $t = 0$, respectively, while $\lambda$ is the decay constant. The decay of the parent produces daughter nuclides $D(t)$, or radiogenics, which is defined as

$$D(t) = N_0 - N(t)\ .$$

Based on those ideas, a group of astronomers investigates a number of meteorite samples to determine their ages. They have two kinds of samples: allende chondrite (A) and basaltic achondrite (B). From the samples, they measure the abundance of $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$ and $^{87}\mathrm{Sr}$, where it is assumed that $^{87}\mathrm{Sr}$ is entirely produced by the decay of $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$. The value of $\lambda$ is $1.42 \times 10^{-11}$ per year for this isotopic decay. In addition, non-radiogenic element $^{86}\mathrm{Sr}$ is also measured. Results of measurement are given in the table below, expressed in ppm (part per million).

| Sample No | Meteorite type | $^{86}\mathrm{Sr}$ (ppm) | $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$ (ppm) | $^{87}\mathrm{Sr}$ (ppm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A | 29.6 | 0.3 | 20.7 |
| 2 | B | 58.7 | 68.5 | 44.7 |
| 3 | B | 74.2 | 14.4 | 52.9 |
| 4 | A | 40.2 | 7.0 | 28.6 |
| 5 | A | 19.7 | 0.4 | 13.8 |
| 6 | B | 37.9 | 31.6 | 28.4 |
| 7 | A | 33.4 | 4.0 | 23.6 |
| 8 | B | 29.8 | 105.0 | 26.4 |
| 9 | A | 9.8 | 0.8 | 6.9 |
| 10 | B | 18.5 | 44.0 | 15.4 |

**Questions:**

parts.statement: Express the time $t$ in term of $\dfrac{D(t)}{N(t)}$
Determine the half-life $t_{1/2}$, i.e., the time needed to obtain a half number of parents after decay.

Knowledge on the ratio between two isotopes is more valuable than just the absolute abundance of each isotope. It is quite likely that there was some initial strontium present. By taking $\left(\frac{^{87}\mathrm{Rb}}{^{86}\mathrm{Sr}}\right)$ as independent variable and $\left(\frac{^{87}\mathrm{Sr}}{^{86}\mathrm{Sr}}\right)$ as dependent variable, estimate the simple linear regression model to represent the data.

Plot $\left(\frac{^{87}\mathrm{Rb}}{^{86}\mathrm{Sr}}\right)$ versus $\left(\frac{^{87}\mathrm{Sr}}{^{86}\mathrm{Sr}}\right)$ and also the regression line (isochrone) for each type of the meteorites. (Please use minimum 7 decimal digits for intermediate calculations)
Subsequently, help this astronomer to determine the age of each type of the meteorites and its error. Which type is older?

answer.value: Type A: (4.816 ± 0.282) × 10^9 year; Type B: (3.595 ± 0.095) × 10^9 year; type A is older.
answer.note: The official solution also prints '= 3.595 ± 0.435 Gyr' for type B, inconsistent with its own ± 0.095 × 10^9 year.

parts.statement: Determine the initial value of $\left(\frac{^{87}\mathrm{Sr}}{^{86}\mathrm{Sr}}\right)_0$ for each type of the meteorites and its error.

problems.statementAfterParts:
*Glossary*:

A simple linear regression line $y=a+bx$ can be fitted to a set of data $(X_{\mathrm{i}},Y_{\mathrm{i}})$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, in which

$$b = \frac{SS_{xy}}{SS_{xx}}$$

$$a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$$

where

$SS_{xx}$ : sum of square for $X = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i^2 - \frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i\right)^2$

$SS_{yy}$ : sum of square for $Y = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i^2 - \frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i\right)^2$

$SS_{xy}$ : sum of square for both $X$ and $Y = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i Y_i - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i$

Standard deviation of each parameter, $a$ and $b$ can be calculated by

$$S_a = \sqrt{\frac{SS_{YY} - \frac{(SS_{XY})^2}{SS_{XX}}}{(n-2)SS_{XX}} \times \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i^2}$$

$$S_b = \sqrt{\frac{SS_{YY} - \frac{(SS_{XY})^2}{SS_{XX}}}{(n-2)SS_{XX}}}$$

figures.caption: Type A
